question: Describe a situation where your first solution didn’t work. How did you iterate?

raiseTranscript.text: I built a simple script to parse logs for a feature launch. It worked on my machine but failed in prod due to encoding differences. I added logging, reproduced the error locally with sample data, then switched to a library that handled encoding.
What did you learn from the first attempt?
I now always test with real prod-like data early instead of assuming my environment matches.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a situation where your first solution didn’t work. How did you iterate?
- Individual task: log parser for feature launch
- First script failed on prod encoding
- Added logging, reproduced locally, switched libraries
Outcome: script worked; learned to test with prod data
Quote: "I now always test with real prod-like data early"
Follow-up: What did you learn? - Explicit reflection on process change
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The competency tested is Problem-Solving & Analytical Thinking on an individual-scope task. Candidate described building a log parser that failed due to encoding, then added logging and switched libraries after local reproduction. The concrete quote about testing with prod-like data early shows they closed the loop from failure to process change. This meets expectations for 0-2 years because ownership stayed on their own work and they incorporated feedback without needing direction. Biggest strength is the clear iteration step tied to a measurable fix.

lowerTranscript.text: My first approach to fix a dashboard bug was to rewrite the query. It still showed wrong numbers so I asked my manager what to try next.
Did you try anything else before asking?
Not really, I wasn’t sure where to look.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a situation where your first solution didn’t work. How did you iterate?
- Individual dashboard bug fix
- First rewrite of query failed
- Immediately escalated without further attempts
Outcome: manager provided next step
Quote: "I wasn’t sure where to look"
Follow-up: Did you try anything else? - No additional debugging shown
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. The competency tested is Problem-Solving & Analytical Thinking. Candidate rewrote a query that still produced wrong numbers then stopped and asked for direction. The quote "I wasn’t sure where to look" reveals absence of personal iteration or root-cause steps. For 0-2 years this falls short because the expectation is coachability plus ownership of one’s own work before escalation. Biggest gap is lack of any diagnostic actions between first failure and seeking help.

raiseTranscript.text: We needed to reduce API latency for a shared service. My initial caching layer added inconsistency across teams. I instrumented metrics, ran A/B tests with two teams, then moved to a read-through cache with invalidation hooks.
What metrics drove the second design?
P99 latency dropped 40% and cache hit rate stabilized at 92% with no cross-team data complaints after rollout.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a situation where your first solution didn’t work. How did you iterate?
- Cross-team API latency reduction
- First caching layer caused inconsistency
- Added metrics, A/B tested, switched to read-through with invalidation
Outcome: 40% P99 drop, 92% hit rate, no complaints
Quote: "cache hit rate stabilized at 92% with no cross-team data complaints"
Follow-up: What metrics drove the second design? - Clear before/after data
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. The competency tested is Problem-Solving & Analytical Thinking with cross-team scope. Candidate’s first caching approach created inconsistency, then they added instrumentation and ran A/B tests before landing on a read-through design. The quote about 40% P99 reduction and 92% hit rate with zero complaints shows iteration produced measurable impact beyond their own team. This meets senior expectations because influence without authority and data-driven pivots are visible. Biggest strength is linking the failed first attempt directly to the metrics that shaped the final solution.

lowerTranscript.text: I tried adding a new index to speed up a shared query. Performance didn’t improve so I reverted it and moved on to other work.
Did you investigate why the index didn’t help?
A bit, but the team was busy so I didn’t dig further.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a situation where your first solution didn’t work. How did you iterate?

- Reverted without deeper analysis
Outcome: moved on to other work
Quote: "the team was busy so I didn’t dig further"

senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. The competency tested is Problem-Solving & Analytical Thinking. Candidate added an index to a shared query, saw no improvement, reverted, and stopped. The quote "the team was busy so I didn’t dig further" indicates limited iteration and no attempt to quantify impact or involve stakeholders. For 3-7 years this is below bar because clearer metrics and cross-team coordination are expected. Biggest gap is absence of any diagnostic loop after the first attempt failed.

raiseTranscript.text: My team’s on-call load was high after a migration. The first playbook we wrote missed several failure modes. I had the team run a blameless postmortem, added runbooks, then created a rotation for updating them quarterly.
How did you handle the engineers who kept getting paged?
I paired the newest engineer with a senior for the first two weeks and tracked their ticket resolution time; it improved 3x.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a situation where your first solution didn’t work. How did you iterate?
- Team on-call load after migration
- First playbook missed failure modes
- Ran postmortem, added runbooks, quarterly update rotation
Outcome: 3x faster resolution for new engineers
Quote: "tracked their ticket resolution time; it improved 3x"
Follow-up: How did you handle the engineers? - Coaching and measurement shown
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. The competency tested is Problem-Solving & Analytical Thinking applied to team outcomes. Candidate’s initial playbook failed to cover failure modes, then they drove a postmortem and created a living runbook process. The quote about 3x resolution improvement after pairing shows they developed people while fixing the process. This meets manager expectations because the iteration produced leverage through the team rather than heroics. Biggest strength is connecting the failed first attempt to both process and people-development changes.

lowerTranscript.text: The team’s deployment script kept failing. I rewrote it myself over a weekend. It worked but the team still asked me to fix issues later.
Did the team own any part of the fix?
Not really, I just wanted it done quickly.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a situation where your first solution didn’t work. How did you iterate?
- Team deployment script failures
- Manager rewrote script personally
- No team involvement in iteration
Outcome: recurring issues, continued escalations
Quote: "I just wanted it done quickly"
Follow-up: Did the team own any part? - No delegation or coaching
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. The competency tested is Problem-Solving & Analytical Thinking. Candidate rewrote a failing deployment script alone; issues continued because the team never owned the solution. The quote "I just wanted it done quickly" reveals focus on personal speed over team leverage. For a manager this falls short because creating leverage through the team and handling underperformance are required. Biggest gap is the absence of any mechanism to transfer ownership after the first attempt failed.

raiseTranscript.text: Our acquisition integration was behind because the first data-migration plan ignored regulatory constraints. I convened the legal, product, and engineering leads, ran scenario planning on three options, then chose a phased approach that delayed revenue by one quarter but avoided compliance risk.
What was the long-term impact on the combined org?
We closed the integration in 11 months instead of the original 9, but retained 95% of key engineers and hit the next-year synergy target.
